bottom_line.headline: Democrats are favored to take the House
bottom_line.detail: Generic ballot D+8.9 (Silver Bulletin, Oct 16); RealClearPolling D+8.0. Cook moved 11 more House races toward Democrats on Oct 16, on top of 18 the week before; it counts 21 toss-ups and its latest published projection (Oct 9) is a Democratic gain of 9–19 seats.

bottom_line.headline: The Senate is a coin flip tilting Democratic — and the holds are not free
bottom_line.detail: Dems need net +4: hold Michigan and Minnesota (both within 3) and win four of six GOP-held toss-ups — Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Alaska. Averages have the Democrat ahead in five; Kansas sits at Marshall +0.3. Lose a hold and it takes five pickups. Markets put a Democratic Senate at 62–65%.

bottom_line.headline: Trump is deeply underwater
bottom_line.detail: Net approval −21 (RealClearPolling) to −22 (Silver Bulletin). This week's polls run from −13 (Rasmussen) to −28 (Fox, AP-NORC); Pew has approval at 30%.

bottom_line.headline: Hochul is comfortably ahead in New York
bottom_line.detail: Up 11–12 on Blakeman (Marist, Emerson) and 9 in Siena's last poll. One small text-message poll last week had it at 3; treat it as an outlier until a major pollster agrees. No new statewide poll this week.

bottom_line.headline: Buffalo and Long Island House seats are settled; NY-17 isn't
bottom_line.detail: Cook: NY-26 (Kennedy) Solid D, NY-01 (LaLota) Solid R, NY-04 (Gillen) Likely D. Lawler vs Conley in the Hudson Valley is the state's only toss-up: Conley 48–46 in the one independent poll. Cook also moved the open North Country seat, NY-21, from Likely R to Lean R on Oct 16.

bottom_line.headline: Your ballot: five towns, one box at the bottom
bottom_line.detail: North Tonawanda, Orchard Park, Scottsville, Dunkirk and Fredonia — Congress, state legislature, county seats and the one proposition (NT's $18M community center). Early voting opens in a week, Oct 24–Nov 1.

what_changed: Ohio: a Bowling Green/YouGov poll (Sep 29–Oct 9, posted Oct 16) has Brown 48–42, and RealClearPolling's average moved to Brown +3.3 from +3.1 — the widest Democratic lead of the six pickups. The four pickups still run through Maine, Ohio and Texas plus one of Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

The holds: Rasmussen (Oct 12–14, Republican-leaning) has El-Sayed 46–44 in Michigan; the average eased to +2.6 from +2.7, and none of the last six polls has Rogers ahead. Minnesota's average widened to Flanagan +2.9 from +2.6 as older polls dropped out of the window. Both holds still stand; both are still inside the margin.

Texas: the University of Texas poll (Sep 25–Oct 5, Talarico 50–47) entered the average, which read Talarico +2.2 against +2.3 yesterday. Alaska widened to Peltola +2.5 from +1.4 and Georgia to Ossoff +9.0 from +8.1 with no new poll in either — September surveys aged out of RealClearPolling's window. Iowa (Turek +0.9), Kansas (Marshall +0.3) and Maine (Jackson +1.6) are effectively unchanged.

House: Cook's Oct 16 note, "Eleven More House Races Shift Toward Democrats," moved Montana's open 1st to Toss Up, Florida's 25th (Moskowitz) from Toss Up to Lean D, Ohio's 1st (Landsman) to Likely D, and New York's open 21st from Likely R to Lean R among them (full list via the Denver Gazette). Cook's toss-up count stays at 21; its Solid R column reads 171, down from the 174 this page carried yesterday.

National: Silver Bulletin's generic ballot rose to D+8.9 from D+8.6; RealClearPolling is steady at D+8.0. Trump's net approval slipped to −20.7 from −20.4 on RealClearPolling as RMG Research (−17) and a new Rasmussen week entered; Silver Bulletin reads −22.3. Polymarket has a Democratic Senate at 64.5%, Kalshi 62.5% (Oct 16).

glossary.text: A poll question that names no candidates: "Would you vote for the Democrat or the Republican for Congress in your district?" Averaged nationally, it is the best single read on which way the House is leaning. D +9 means Democrats lead by about 9 points. For scale, 2018's blue wave was about D +8 and Democrats gained 41 seats; 2022 was roughly R +3 and Republicans barely took the House.
The share of adults who approve of the president minus the share who disapprove. Negative means more people disapprove. Presidents with net approval this low usually lose seats in a midterm.

Race ratings from the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan handicapper. Toss Up means either side could win; Lean is a slight edge; Likely a clear one; Solid is not in doubt. Ratings move when polls or candidates change. Sabato's Crystal Ball (University of Virginia) is a similar nonpartisan handicapper; when it differs from Cook, the race note says so.

Prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi) let people bet real money on outcomes; the price is the crowd's probability. 64% means the market thinks Democrats win the Senate about two times in three. It is a forecast, not a poll.

The Senate is 53 Republicans to 47 Democrats (counting two independents who vote with Democrats). Democrats need a net gain of four seats for 51. That means holding every seat they have now — Michigan and Minnesota are the close ones, Georgia and New Hampshire less so — and winning four of the six Republican-held toss-ups: Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Alaska. A "hold" is keeping a seat you already have; a "pickup" is taking one from the other party. Lose a hold and the number becomes five pickups.

The headline number for each Senate race is RealClearPolling's average of recent polls, which is steadier than any single survey. The note under it lists the latest individual polls. "Republican-leaning" or "Democratic-leaning" after a pollster means the firm works for that party or has a record of tilting that way — weigh those lighter.

Every poll is a sample. A typical one is accurate to about 3–5 points either way, so a 2-point lead is a coin flip and even a 6-point lead can flip. Averages of several polls are steadier than any one poll.

In the Senate section the bar runs from the middle: blue to the left for a Democratic lead, red to the right for a Republican one, longer for a bigger lead. In the governor section the two bars run toward each other and the gap is undecided voters.

outlook.title: What could still change this
outlook.lede: The October surprise already happened, in February: the Iran war. It is the main reason the president's net approval sits around −20 instead of the −10 range he held at New Year's, and nothing in the next three weeks is likely to swing the national mood that far again. So the question is not whether a shock changes the House — at D+8.6 that would take a very large one — but whether anything tips the four to six Senate seats sitting inside the margin of error.

items.why: A ceasefire, a major casualty event or an escalation is the one thing that could move national numbers several points in either direction. Everything else is small by comparison.
Gas is the number voters feel directly. A spike in the last two weeks hurts the party in power; a drop helps a little.
Texas and Maine are within a couple of points, so one bad week for a candidate — a scandal, a debate stumble — can decide a seat.
Early voting starts Oct 24. The first week's turnout in the toss-up states is the first real signal; prediction markets react to it before the polls do.

outlook.noise: What usually matters less than it looks: a late rally blitz (it fires up both bases) and any single surprising poll. Ignore it unless an average moves.

how_to_read.title: How to read this without panicking
items: A lead of 2 points is a tie. A lead of 5 is a real edge, not a lock. Polls miss by 3–5 points in a normal year.
One poll means almost nothing. The averages on this page are what to watch, and they move slowly on purpose.
Headlines say "Democrats worry" because worry gets clicks. Check it against the numbers below before you believe it.
What would actually be bad news: the averages moving 3 or more points toward Republicans across several states at once. One state wobbling is noise.
The Senate may not be known on election night (see Election night, below). A slow count is not a bad count.

election_night.title: What to expect on election night
election_night.intro: Polls close in waves; counts finish on each state's own schedule. Here is what is normal, so a slow result doesn't read as a bad one.

items.what: New York (governor, NY-17, NY-26 and the local races) and most of the East count fast. North Carolina, Georgia and Ohio usually report the bulk of their vote within a few hours of polls closing.

Pennsylvania counts fast, and four of its House seats cover every fault line in the country: PA-1 (Fitzpatrick, Philadelphia suburbs), PA-7 (Mackenzie, Lehigh Valley and Latino Allentown), PA-8 (Bresnahan, Scranton), PA-10 (Perry, central PA). The Times' rule of thumb: Democrats flip all four, it's a wave; flip none, the polls were wrong. Two or three is the expected night. Trump's approval in the state is 34% (Times/Inquirer/Siena).
Texas, Iowa and Kansas typically have near-complete counts by midnight Eastern. Michigan and Minnesota can run into the early morning when close.

Maine: if nobody clears 50% of first choices (write-in candidates make that likely), the ranked-choice count happens in Augusta and took about nine days in June's primary. Alaska: by law the ranked-choice tabulation is Nov 18 and by-mail ballots count if postmarked by Nov 3, so a close race there waits two weeks.
If the Senate comes down to Maine or Alaska, control may not be known until mid-November. That is the calendar, not a sign anything went wrong.
